sections.title: How does the 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator work?
sections.html:
The 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total buying cost in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the printer model and the filament); then you type in the volume of your 3D model, the slicing software cost, the total labor cost and the extra 3D printer accessories.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total buying cost=(extra 3D printer accessories + total electrical cost + filament density × filament price × volume of your 3D model × how many models do you want to print? + slicing software cost + 3D modeling cost + printer price)
Equipment power consumption=(-electricity cost × heated bed × time using heated bed mode + 1000 × total electrical cost) ÷ (electricity cost × usage time)
Total outsourcing cost=3D modeling cost + how many models do you want to print? × outsourcing price per model + shipping cost
Total manufacturing cost=(extra 3D printer accessories + total electrical cost + filament density × filament price × volume of your 3D model × how many models do you want to print? + total labor cost + slicing software cost + 3D modeling cost + printer price)
Total outsourcing cost=(3D modeling cost + how many models do you want to print? × outsourcing price per model + shipping outsourcing cost)
How many models do you want to print?=(-total shipping cost to your clients + total selling price) ÷ your selling price per model

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the volume of your 3D model, the slicing software cost and the total labor cost — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total buying cost, derived from the volume of your 3D model, the slicing software cost and the total labor cost. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the volume of your 3D model, the slicing software cost, the total labor cost and the extra 3D printer accessories, which is 26 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter printer price in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Printer price opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Printer price = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the 3D printer - buy vs outsource calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
